interactions.label: A 26-year-old woman has an estimated blood loss of 400 mL following vaginal deli

params.question: A 26-year-old woman has an estimated blood loss of 400 mL following vaginal delivery. She is tachycardic at 112 bpm with a blood pressure of 88/58 mmHg. How should this presentation be classified?

answers.text: Not PPH, as blood loss has not reached the 500 mL threshold

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The 500 mL volume criterion is only one arm of the definition. Any blood loss causing haemodynamic instability — tachycardia and hypotension here — meets the clinical threshold for PPH regardless of estimated volume.

A pulse of 112 bpm and BP of 88/58 mmHg indicate uncompensated haemodynamic instability, not compensated loss. Moreover, visual estimation underestimates true blood loss by 30–50%, so the actual volume is likely higher.

answers.text: PPH, because haemodynamic instability defines the clinical threshold regardless of estimated volume

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The clinical definition of PPH includes any blood loss that produces haemodynamic instability, irrespective of measured volume — visual estimation consistently underestimates true loss by 30–50%.

answers.text: Secondary PPH, as the bleeding occurred after placental delivery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Secondary PPH refers to haemorrhage between 24 hours and 12 weeks postpartum, not simply 'after placental delivery'. Bleeding within the first 24 hours is primary PPH, which is the more common and dangerous form.

overallFeedback.feedback: PPH is defined not only by volume (≥500 mL vaginal, ≥1000 mL caesarean) but also by any blood loss causing haemodynamic instability. Tachycardia and hypotension demand immediate treatment regardless of the estimated volume.

Exactly right. In clinical practice, always treat haemodynamic instability as PPH — do not wait for a volume threshold to be crossed, especially since visual estimation underestimates blood loss by 30–50%.

params.question: You are managing atonic PPH unresponsive to initial uterotonics. You initiate bimanual uterine compression. Which statement best describes how this technique controls haemorrhage?

answers.text: It stimulates the Ferguson reflex, triggering endogenous oxytocin release from the posterior pituitary

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The Ferguson reflex is triggered by cervical and vaginal distension during labour, not by bimanual compression of the uterine body. Bimanual compression works by direct mechanical tamponade, not via a neuroendocrine reflex.

answers.text: It evacuates retained clots from the uterine cavity, allowing uterotonics to reach the myometrium

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While clot evacuation may be a secondary benefit, the primary mechanism is direct mechanical compression of the placental bed vessels between the two hands — substituting for the myometrial contraction that is failing.

answers.text: It compresses the uterine body between the vaginal and abdominal hands, mechanically occluding the placental bed vessels

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The internal hand in the vaginal fornix and the external hand on the fundus compress the uterus between them, directly occluding the placental bed vessels — the same 'living ligatures' principle that myometrial contraction normally provides.

answers.text: It stretches the lower uterine segment, activating a myotatic reflex that initiates uterine contraction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: There is no myotatic reflex mechanism in uterine smooth muscle analogous to skeletal muscle stretch reflexes. Bimanual compression is a direct mechanical tamponade, not a contraction trigger.

overallFeedback.feedback: Bimanual compression works by sandwiching the uterus between an internal vaginal hand and an external abdominal hand, directly compressing the placental bed vessels. This exploits the 'living ligatures' principle — the same mechanism that myometrial contraction normally uses to achieve haemostasis.

Well done. Bimanual compression is a no-equipment, immediately available technique that provides a mechanical substitute for failing myometrial contraction — always used alongside continuing uterotonic therapy.

params.question: In acute uterine inversion, the cervical ring gradually relaxes over time, making delayed manual reduction easier than immediate reduction.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. The cervical ring progressively constricts around the inverted fundus over time, making delayed reduction far more difficult than immediate reduction. Every minute of delay allows the constriction ring to tighten further, which is why uterine inversion demands immediate recognition and action.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. The cervical ring progressively tightens around the inverted fundus with every passing minute, making reduction increasingly difficult. This is precisely why immediate recognition and reduction are critical; delay worsens the constriction and compounds the cardiovascular collapse.
